newsitem.title: USA: Korean airline crash victim dies at Texas hospital.
newsitem.headline: Korean airline crash victim dies at Texas hospital.

text.p: An 11-year-old girl severely burned in last week's deadly Korean Air plane crash on the Pacific island of Guam has died at a U.S. military hospital.
Three other crash survivors being treated for burns at Brooke Army Medical Center in San Antonio, Texas, were in critical condition, a hospital spokesman said on Monday.
The girl, Grace Chung, died on Sunday after undergoing four hours of surgery for burns over 45 percent of her body.
She was a U.S. citizen from Marietta, Georgia, whose family immigrated from Taiwan. Her mother, brother and sister all died in the air crash.
Chung and others were flown on Saturday to the San Antonio hospital, which has a state-of-the-art burn treatment center.
The three other survivors were identified as SeJin Ju, 28, Kyu HeeHan, 29, and Young Hak Jung, 39, all Koreans.
Korean Air Lines Flight 801, with 254 people on board, slammed into hillside jungle three miles (five km) from Guam's International airport on Wednesday.
Among the 28 survivors were three Americans, one Japanese and one New Zealander. The rest were South Koreans, KAL said.
Officials of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), said on Sunday that 140 bodies had been recovered and were awaiting identification. Most of the other remains were badly mangled.

"We are prepared to repatriate the remains of South Koreans killed in the crash. Some relatives want immediate repatriation while others want to wait until all the remains are identified," a Korean Air spokesman said.

NTSB officials said preliminary examination of the engines, the wreckage and data from the flight recorders showed that the plane was in full control on a steady descent and the crew was not aware of any impending disaster.

The NTSB, which is also looking into the possibility that an unusually heavy downpour and sudden loss of visibility could have contributed to the crash, has not determined whether human error was the cause.
The Seoul government said on Monday it planned to set up a $118 million medical center to cope with disasters requiring urgent medical attention.

"The medical center could provide quick medical support to people requiring emergency treatment after plane crashes, building collapses, landslides or other calamities," said Yoo Keun-hyock, a Health and Welfare Ministry official.
He said the ministry, in cooperation with other government agencies, planned to present a bill to set up the center to parliament this year.
